opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The biggest change in the second generation is that we stopped treating randomness as noise to be eliminated and started treating it as the normal condition of the task.

With the first-generation model, tabletop tidying worked well when the scene resembled what it had seen in training: objects in familiar positions, reasonable lighting, a clear order of operations. But a real table is messy in an open-ended way. A cup might be tipped over, a pen might be half under a notebook, someone might have left a wrapper in a spot you'd never anticipate. When the scene drifted from the training distribution, the old model tended to commit to a plan too early, and if the first grasp failed or an object shifted, it often didn't recover gracefully. It would hesitate, repeat the same failed motion, or lose track of what was left to do.

The second generation improves on this in a few ways.

First, it reasons in a closed loop much more tightly. Instead of predicting a long trajectory and executing it blindly, it keeps re-reading the scene and adjusting as it goes. If something slides when the gripper touches it, the model treats that as new information rather than as a failure of the plan.

Second, the data is much more diverse, and deliberately so. We put a lot of effort into collecting episodes with perturbations, partial failures and recoveries, cluttered and odd configurations. So the model has actually seen what it looks like to fail a grasp and try again from a different angle, rather than only seeing clean, successful demonstrations.

Third, there's a better separation between deciding what to do next and deciding how to physically do it. At a higher level, the model decides that the cup should be righted before the napkin is moved. At a lower level, it handles the fine motor details. That makes it much more robust to randomness, because a surprise at the motor level doesn't derail the overall task understanding.

The practical result is that the robot feels less brittle. It isn't perfect, and there are still long-tail situations that trip it up. But the behavior has gone from "works when the setup is right" to "keeps making sensible progress even when the setup is wrong." For tidying, that's really the whole game, because no two tables are ever messy in the same way.

r001.rationale: The response says the second-generation robot keeps making progress on messy, open-ended tables with cluttered and odd configurations, communicating that it can tidy from varied, randomly arranged starting scenes.

r002.rationale: It says the robot adjusts when an object shifts during its own interaction, but does not state that it adapts to location changes made by a person while it is working.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that the robot notices or skips tidying actions a person has already completed alongside it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest shift is that the second generation stopped treating randomness as a problem to be eliminated and started treating it as something the model has to live with and reason through.

With the first generation, we were essentially fitting demonstrations. If the tabletop looked like what the robot had seen in training, it did fine. But a tidying task is almost adversarially random. The cup is upside down, the cable is tangled around the stapler, someone left a half-eaten sandwich there. Every arrangement is new. The first-generation model would often freeze or do something confidently wrong, because it had memorized trajectories rather than understanding what "tidy" means.

So in the second generation we made three changes. First, the model perceives the scene as a set of objects with relationships, not as a single image to be mapped to an action. That means when the arrangement changes, the representation changes gracefully rather than falling off a cliff. Second, we trained it to plan at the level of subgoals, like "clear the surface, group similar things, put the fragile items last," and let the low-level policy figure out the specific grasps. That hierarchy absorbs a lot of the randomness, because the high-level plan stays stable even when the details shift. Third, and this is the part I'm most happy with, the model is allowed to be uncertain. If a grasp fails or an object slides, it re-observes and re-plans instead of blindly replaying the rest of the sequence.

The honest result is that it's slower on the easy cases than a scripted system would be, but it recovers on the messy cases, and the messy cases are what a real home is made of. That's the improvement that matters to me.

r001.rationale: The response says the second-generation model handles tidying across new, randomly arranged tabletop scenes and messy cases.

r002.rationale: It describes adapting when arrangements change or objects slide, but does not state that it responds to people changing object locations while it is working.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention skipping actions a person has already completed alongside the robot.

astra-6.text: I’d say the major improvement is that it can adapt to what actually happens, rather than relying on everything happening exactly as planned. When you’re tidying a tabletop, objects can start in different positions, and moving one object can shift another. The important thing is to reassess the scene and adjust the next action. So it’s less about eliminating randomness and more about handling it without losing track of the task.

r001.rationale: It says the robot can adjust while tidying when objects start in different positions, conveying that it can handle a randomly arranged tabletop.

r002.rationale: It describes objects shifting when another object is moved, but does not say the robot adapts to location changes made by a person.

r003.rationale: It does not state that the robot skips actions a person has already completed.

The second-generation model can look at what actually happened and adjust its next move, instead of depending on a fixed sequence. That makes it more reliable when the situation changes.
